However, among the rest of the diversions repared for king James, there was, to be sure, one red ion, made of plaster, at Linlithgow, and certainly, the ad- dress of this lion, in which was enclosed James Wiseman, schoolmaster of the said town, was better worth attention, than any other of the northern recreations. “ Thrice royal sir, here I do you beseech, Who art a lion, hear a Jion’s speech; A miracle, for, since the days of Esop, No lion, till these times, his voice dared raise up To such a majesty; then, king of men, The king of beasts speaks to thee fram his den,
Who (though he now be here enclosed in plaster), When he is free, is Lithgow’s wise schoolmaster.”

Whilst his majesty was absent, the queen dreamed a very fearful dream,' respecting his perscnal safety, and despatched a special messenger with the partieulars of it, begging him withal to hasten home to her. For once in his life, king James paid no heed to the call of superstition; perhaps, in regard to the supernatural, he attended to the crotchets of no brain but his own, for he did not particularly hasten his homeward progress.

Her majesty sojourned at Greenwich Palace during the king’s absence. The young gentlewomen of Ladies’ Hall, a great boarding-school at the noighbouring town .of Deptford, performed a masque for the diversion of her ma- jesty. In the course of the prologue the queen was thus addressed :-—

“ The lovely crew Of Lady’s Hall, a pure academy, *» Where modesty doth sway as governess, These pretty nimps (nymphs) devoted to your grace, Present a sport, which they do yearly celebrate On Candlemas night, with due solemnity, And great applause.”

Hymen was the hero of the masque, but the instructors at Ladics’ Hall considered it only proper that so impertinent a god as Cupid should be banished from all association with that ‘respectable divinity. All cupids being contra- band articles at the Deptforde school, patronized by her majesty queen Anne, and the court at Greenwich. The
iece was therefore entitled “ Cupid’s Banishment,” and eing written under the immediate surveillance of Mr.

She descants still on chastity ; The diapason of her tone is ‘ Cupid’s gone.’ He’s gone, he’s gone, he’s quite exiled ! Venus’ brat, peevish imp, Fancy’s child, Let him go! let him go! with his quiver and his bow.” In the course of the masque a concert was performed, con- sidered unrivalled. Twelve young ladies as nymphs entered, dressed all in white, their hair hanging down their necks, adorned with jewels, necklaces on their heads, and coronets of artificial flowers, with a puff of tinsie rising in the midst. They ’ paced towards her majesty, and after the first strain of the violins, commenced dancing “Anna Regina in letters.” That is, as they stood or moved, linked hand in hand, they formed a figure which constantly presented to the eyes of the beholder the queen’s written name. Their. second dance was “Jacobus Rex,” in compliment to the king, then Carolus P., for prince Charles, “ with many excellent figures falling off, devised by Mr. Ounslo, tutor to Ladies’ Tffall,” who was doubtless a most exalted personage that night, in his own opinion. The poets in ey ene offered many tributes .to her memory. Camden has’ preserved tivo elegiac epitaphs, which possess some elegance of thought:

Eprraro on ANNE oF DENMARK." “ March, with his winds, hath struck a cedar tall, And weeping April mourns that cedar’s fall ; And May intends no flowers her month shall bring, Since she must lose the flower of all the spring: Thps March’s winds hath caused April’s showers, And yet sad May must lose her flower of flowers.”
Another, in which is an allusion to the comet, supposed to forebode her death:

“ Thee to invite, th@great God sent a star ; His nearest frien} and kin good princes are, Who, though they run their race of man and die, Death serves but to refine their.majesty ; So did our queen her court from hence remove, And left this earth, to be enthroned above ; Then she is changed, not dead,—no good prince dies, But, Jike the sun, doth only set to rise.”

The king arrived at Greenwich a few days after his queen’s funcral. _“ All her coffers and cabinets were brought from Somerset Iouse, in four carts, and delivered, by in- ventory, to his majesty, by sir Edward Coke and the queen’s auditor. The king examined all. Ile found that the queen had received from Herrick, her jeweller,’ thirty-six thousand pounds’ worth of jewels, of which no vestige appeared. The jeweller produced the models, and swore to the delivery of the property. Pierrot, the queen’s French attendant, and her favourite maid, Danish Anna, were suspected of the embezzlement of these jewels, and of a vast mass of ready money, which their royal mistress was supposed to have hoarded. Both were examined, and afterwards committed to the custody of justice Doubleday, to be privately impri- soned in his fois: But it does not appear that any trace was ever gained of the missing treasure.” *

the reign of James I. It was destroyed, during the civil wars, with many a funeral memento of more durable ma- terials. She had no other monument. Her death occurred in the forty-sixth year of her age. She left but two living children, Charles, prince of Wales, afterwards Charles I, and Elizabeth, queen of Bohemia, both of theni singularly unfortunate. James I. survived his consort seven years; he never enconraged the idea of a second marriage; but the manners of his court became extremely gross and unrefined, for ladies no longer came there, after the death of Anne of Denmark. ~
